power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Learning Health Systems (LHSs) have considerable potential to improve the implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-informed health interventions.
However, practical guidance on operationalising LHS principles across diverse health system contexts, levels (macro, meso, and micro), and stakeholder groups remains limited.

To support broader adoption, the World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with the University of Newcastle's National Centre of Implementation Science (NCOIS), developed a draft Guidance on using a Learning Health System approach to implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-informed health interventions (Guidance).
An international stakeholder consultation was undertaken to inform its refinement.

The consultation sought feedback to: (1) assess the relevance and applicability of the draft Guidance; (2) identify implementation considerations across diverse settings; and (3) obtain recommendations to improve its content, usability, and practical application.

Process Stakeholders from policymaking, research, clinical, and other health system sectors across all six WHO regions were invited by the https://www.who.int/initiatives/evidence-informed-policy-network to attend a two-hour online workshop conducted in April 2025 via Zoom.
text.formatted: Process Stakeholders from policymaking, research, clinical, and other health system sectors across all six WHO regions were invited by the <ref type="url" target="https://www.who.int/initiatives/evidence-informed-policy-network">WHO Evidence-Informed   Policy Network (EVIPNet)</ref> to attend a two-hour online workshop conducted in April 2025 via Zoom.

text.text: Participants received background materials in advance.
Facilitated breakout discussions focused on: (1) content and structure; and (2) dissemination, implementation, and practical application.
Feedback was collected from multiple sources (e.g., discussion notes, Zoom chats) and synthesised by NCOIS staff involved in the Guidance development.
Participants expressed strong support for the purpose and value of the Guidance.
Feedback emphasised the need for flexible, iterative approaches that accommodate variation in health system contexts, levels, stakeholder needs, and available resources.

Participants highlighted the importance of supporting progressive development of LHS capabilities and strongly endorsed accessible language, case studies, practical tools, and alignment with existing WHO frameworks.
Feedback informed refinements to improve clarity, accessibility, and practical applicability.

Revisions strengthened content on LHS concepts, implementation, leadership and governance, stakeholder engagement, and equity, while adding case studies, implementation tools, resource inventories, and practical supports.
The consultation provided a robust mechanism to assess and strengthen the relevance, usability, feasibility, and acceptability of the Guidance.
The resulting refinements enhanced its applicability across diverse settings and its potential to support implementation, scale-up and sustainment using an LHS approach.

Globally, health-care spending is on an unsustainable trajectory: projections indicate total outlays will rise from about US$9.2 trillion in 2019 to US$16.9 trillion by 2050, increasing faster than the world economy and thus claiming a larger share of global GDP (1, 2).
text.formatted: Globally, health-care spending is on an unsustainable trajectory: projections indicate total outlays will rise from about US$9.2 trillion in 2019 to US$16.9 trillion by 2050, increasing faster than the world economy and thus claiming a larger share of global GDP <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref>.

text.text: Yet much of the health burdens experienced by individuals, communities, and the health system can be averted with the evidence already available.
For example, half of all cancers could be prevented if effective cancer prevention and management interventions were routinely implemented at a population level (3).
text.formatted: For example, half of all cancers could be prevented if effective cancer prevention and management interventions were routinely implemented at a population level <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: However, only 14% of effective interventions are ever routinely implemented (even fewer at scale) and on average, it takes 17 years for this to occur (4, 5).
text.formatted: However, only 14% of effective interventions are ever routinely implemented (even fewer at scale) and on average, it takes 17 years for this to occur <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5)</ref>.

text.text: The translation of evidence into practice is impeded by a misalignment between the research conducted and enduser needs, the local context where an intervention is to be implemented (compatibility, adaptability), and the capacity of the setting where the implementation will take place (financing, workforce, supply chains, data) (1, 6, 7).
text.formatted: The translation of evidence into practice is impeded by a misalignment between the research conducted and enduser needs, the local context where an intervention is to be implemented (compatibility, adaptability), and the capacity of the setting where the implementation will take place (financing, workforce, supply chains, data) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7)</ref>.

text.text: 'Learning Health Systems' (LHS) integrate evidence generation, data use and decision-making within health system processes (8).
text.formatted: 'Learning Health Systems' (LHS) integrate evidence generation, data use and decision-making within health system processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8)</ref>.

text.text: Interest in LHSs has grown due to their potential to accelerate the translation of evidence into practice using cycles of continuous improvement (9).
text.formatted: Interest in LHSs has grown due to their potential to accelerate the translation of evidence into practice using cycles of continuous improvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref>.

text.text: However, despite this potential, there remains a notable lag in the use of LHS approaches for implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-based innovations (10) (11) (12).
text.formatted: However, despite this potential, there remains a notable lag in the use of LHS approaches for implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-based innovations <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Whilst LHS models and frameworks exist, they largely focus on the characteristics and core components (12) (13) (14) (15) (16) and few provide practical guidance on applying an LHS approach to implementation, scale-up and sustainment (8, 12).
text.formatted: Whilst LHS models and frameworks exist, they largely focus on the characteristics and core components <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(15)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16)</ref> and few provide practical guidance on applying an LHS approach to implementation, scale-up and sustainment <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, although existing models acknowledge that LHS approaches may require adaptations for diverse settings, there is limited practical guidance on how to translate LHS principles into action to support implementation, scale-up and sustainment efforts across varying health system contexts (10, 12).
text.formatted: Additionally, although existing models acknowledge that LHS approaches may require adaptations for diverse settings, there is limited practical guidance on how to translate LHS principles into action to support implementation, scale-up and sustainment efforts across varying health system contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">12)</ref>.

text.text: This gap is important because the factors influencing implementation, scale-up and sustainment vary across settings (10).
text.formatted: This gap is important because the factors influencing implementation, scale-up and sustainment vary across settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Effective application of an LHS approach requires consideration of local priorities, governance arrangements, workforce capability, stakeholder partnerships, infrastructure and resources (12, 17, 18).
text.formatted: Effective application of an LHS approach requires consideration of local priorities, governance arrangements, workforce capability, stakeholder partnerships, infrastructure and resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">18)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, those who work to improve health systems or services through the better implementation, scale-up and sustainment of effective health policies, programs or interventions require practical guidance on how to apply and adapt LHS principles in their own context (8).
text.formatted: Consequently, those who work to improve health systems or services through the better implementation, scale-up and sustainment of effective health policies, programs or interventions require practical guidance on how to apply and adapt LHS principles in their own context <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(8)</ref>.

text.text: An international stakeholder consultation was undertaken with researchers, policymakers, health system leaders, practitioners and WHO representatives to inform refinement of the draft Guidance.

1. assess the relevance and applicability of the draft Guidance 2. identify implementation considerations across different settings 3. obtain recommendations for improving guidance content and usability

An initial stakeholder engagement meeting, facilitated by WHO and involving representatives from WHO departments, regional offices, and country offices, was convened to establish the scope and direction of the Guidance.
An editorial board was subsequently formed to oversee its development.

A systematic review and synthesis of LHS, implementation, scale-up and sustainment frameworks was then undertaken to inform the development of a WHO LHS framework (10), which provided the foundation for the first draft of the Guidance.
text.formatted: A systematic review and synthesis of LHS, implementation, scale-up and sustainment frameworks was then undertaken to inform the development of a WHO LHS framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>, which provided the foundation for the first draft of the Guidance.

text.text: The draft outlined the infrastructure required to support an LHS focused on implementation, scale-up and sustainment, and described a three-phase, multistep improvement process through which this infrastructure could be operationalised.

The draft Guidance was subsequently presented during an enduser consultation meeting, facilitated by WHO and involving representatives from WHO departments, regional offices, and country offices, to obtain feedback on its content, applicability, and usability.
This consultation forms the focus of the present report.

Stakeholders were invited to participate in the consultation to provide feedback on the draft WHO Learning Health System (LHS) Guidance to improve implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-informed health interventions.

Twenty-five stakeholders were selected to reflect the range of intended users and contributors to the Guidance, including representatives from WHO headquarters and regional offices, policymakers, researchers with expertise in learning health systems and implementation science, and practitioners involved in health system strengthening and evidence-informed decision-making.
Stakeholders represented multiple sectors relevant to the development and application of the Guidance and were drawn from the six WHO regions.
Invitations were distributed via email by the https://www.who.int/initiatives/evidence-informed-policy-network which supports the systematic use of evidence in health policy and decision-making.
text.formatted: Invitations were distributed via email by the <ref type="url" target="https://www.who.int/initiatives/evidence-informed-policy-network">WHO Evidence-Informed Policy   Network (EVIPNet),</ref> which supports the systematic use of evidence in health policy and decision-making.

text.text: Invitees received information about the purpose of the consultation and the draft Guidance, together with materials to support their review and participation.
This consultation formed part of the WHO guidance development process and was undertaken as a quality assurance and stakeholder engagement activity.
As such, this work was exempt from formal human research ethics review.

The consultation was conducted on 1 April 2025 via a two-hour online workshop using the Zoom videoconferencing platform, and was jointly facilitated by NCOIS, WHO and the Centre for Evidence and Implementation (CEI) which was engaged by NCOIS to support workshop facilitation.

Preparatory activities included development of the consultation agenda, consultation questions, participant briefing materials, facilitation resources, and documentation templates to support structured feedback collection.

Prior to the consultation, participants received an email containing background materials, including the consultation objectives, agenda, draft Guidance content, conceptual representations of the proposed framework, supporting literature on LHSs, illustrative case studies, an inventory of potential implementation tools, and an example WHO guidance document on a different topic to demonstrate the intended format and presentation.
The consultation comprised a combination of plenary presentations and smallgroup breakout discussions.
The consultation commenced with an overview of the consultation objectives, the LHS concept, and the development process and content of the draft Guidance.

Participants then engaged in two rounds of breakout discussions focused on: (1) the content, structure, and proposed components of the Guidance; and (2) considerations related to presentation, dissemination, implementation, and practical application of the Guidance.
Breakout discussions were organised to facilitate perspectives from different stakeholder groups, including researchers, WHO staff, and policymakers.
Each group included stakeholders from diverse geographic regions.
Facilitators from NCOIS and CEI guided discussions, encouraged participation, and documented feedback.
The workshop concluded with a plenary session summarising key points raised and outlining next steps in the Guidance development process.
Feedback was collected from multiple sources throughout the consultation process.
During breakout discussions, facilitators documented key discussion points through structured notetaking.
Participants were also able to provide input using virtual whiteboards with digital sticky-note functionality and through the Zoom chat function.
Session recordings were used to verify and supplement notes where required.
Additional feedback was captured through participant annotations, comments, and observations provided during workshop discussions and plenary sessions.
These multiple feedback sources were used to identify areas of agreement, clarify suggested modifications to the draft Guidance, and inform its subsequent refinement.
Feedback was collated and synthesised by NCOIS staff involved in the development of the Guidance.

Comments were categorised according to consultation objectives and reviewed to identify recurring recommendations, implementation considerations, areas of agreement, and suggested revisions to the Guidance.
Below, we summarise feedback and provide quotes to illustrate feedback given by consultation members.
Stakeholders expressed strong support for the overall concept and purpose of the Guidance.
Stakeholders agreed that an LHS approach provides a useful framework for supporting evidence-informed implementation, scale-up and sustainment activities across a range of health system settings.

While there was broad agreement regarding the value of the proposed approach, stakeholders emphasised health systems differ considerably in their governance structures, resources, priorities, and capacities, and therefore the Guidance should provide practical support for flexible and iterative application to allow adaptation for local contexts.
"This approach is relevant in all contexts when we start with identifying the problem with consumers and others -gets everyone on the same page."
"LHS is relevant in any context.
Maybe you don't need something as robust as an LHS to solve every problem, but you can still apply the principles."
"The emphasis on certain components might … need more contextualising within low resource settings."
Stakeholders identified several factors that may influence implementation of the Guidance across countries and health systems.
Stakeholders emphasised the importance of leadership, governance, resourcing, workforce capability, stakeholder partnerships, and mechanisms for generating and using evidence (18, 19).
text.formatted: Stakeholders emphasised the importance of leadership, governance, resourcing, workforce capability, stakeholder partnerships, and mechanisms for generating and using evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">19)</ref>.

text.text: These factors were viewed as foundational elements for establishing and sustaining LHSs.

However, stakeholders highlighted that infrastructure, technical capability, workforce capacity, and organisational maturity vary across different levels of systems (macro -policy-level, meso -district-or regional-level, microlocal facility/ organisational or community-level) and stakeholder groups (e.g., policymakers, researchers, clinicians) (13).
text.formatted: However, stakeholders highlighted that infrastructure, technical capability, workforce capacity, and organisational maturity vary across different levels of systems (macro -policy-level, meso -district-or regional-level, microlocal facility/ organisational or community-level) and stakeholder groups (e.g., policymakers, researchers, clinicians) <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13)</ref>.

text.text: Several stakeholders emphasised the importance of the Guidance supporting implementation approaches that reflect local needs, capacities, and resources and to assist countries and organisations to progressively develop LHS capabilities over time (11).
text.formatted: Several stakeholders emphasised the importance of the Guidance supporting implementation approaches that reflect local needs, capacities, and resources and to assist countries and organisations to progressively develop LHS capabilities over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, stakeholders expressed strong support for the development of WHO guidance on the application of LHS principles to support implementation, scaleup and sustainment and acknowledged the relevance, value and practicality of the proposed approach for supporting evidence-informed improvement activities within health systems.

Feedback highlighted the importance of contextual adaptation, consideration of implementation requirements across different settings, and improvements to the content, format, and usability of the Guidance.
These recommendations informed subsequent revisions to the draft Guidance and supporting resources.
The feedback provided included both overarching suggestions and specific recommendations to revise, expand or consolidate elements of the draft Guidance.
Major revisions incorporated into the updated version focused on enhancing clarity, usability and applicability across diverse health system contexts.

This included simplification of the language and tone to ensure accessibility to a broad range of end-users and strengthening explanations of LHS concepts, processes and their relationship to implementation, scale-up and sustainment activities (20).
text.formatted: This included simplification of the language and tone to ensure accessibility to a broad range of end-users and strengthening explanations of LHS concepts, processes and their relationship to implementation, scale-up and sustainment activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(20)</ref>.

text.text: Practical guidance on applying the LHS approach in a flexible, iterative and contextually relevant manner was integrated throughout the Guidance to support its implementation across different health system levels, settings and resource environments (21).
text.formatted: Practical guidance on applying the LHS approach in a flexible, iterative and contextually relevant manner was integrated throughout the Guidance to support its implementation across different health system levels, settings and resource environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(21)</ref>.

text.text: Specific advice about how to utilise existing structures and processes to best support LHS functions within low-resource settings was included.

Content relating to stakeholder engagement, governance and leadership, and equity was expanded and strengthened, while additional guidance was included on common barriers and enablers to LHS development and strategies for addressing them (12).
text.formatted: Content relating to stakeholder engagement, governance and leadership, and equity was expanded and strengthened, while additional guidance was included on common barriers and enablers to LHS development and strategies for addressing them <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Links to existing relevant frameworks and WHO resources were expanded to complement existing health system improvement efforts.

To support practical application, the Guidance was further enhanced through the inclusion of additional case studies, an inventory of resources, implementation tools, checklists and worksheets designed to support the development and operation of an LHS (10).
text.formatted: To support practical application, the Guidance was further enhanced through the inclusion of additional case studies, an inventory of resources, implementation tools, checklists and worksheets designed to support the development and operation of an LHS <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Table 1 summarises the feedback and subsequent revisions to the Guidance.
Table1.

Consultation feedback and Guidance revisions Consultation feedback Resulting revisions to the Guidance Simplification and clarification of LHS concepts  Simplified language throughout the document  Expanded explanations of LHS concepts and processes  Clarified relationships with quality improvement and implementation approaches  Incorporated practical examples, case studies, summaries and visual aids Adaptability across contexts and health system levels  Added guidance on contextual adaptation across health system levels and settings  Emphasised flexibility in applying LHS principles  Incorporated advice for resourceconstrained contexts  Included practical checklists, worksheets and "short on resources?"

recommendations Strengthening stakeholder engagement and co-design  Expanded content describing stakeholder engagement, consumer involvement, co-design, co-production and co-creation approaches  Provided practical guidance, tools and case studies Need for stronger evidence and practical examples  Added case studies from multiple countries, settings and health system levels  Strengthened discussion of impacts, implementation outcomes and health system benefits.

Alignment with existing frameworks and practices  Clarified how LHS approaches complement and link to existing improvement, implementation and evidence-informed decision-making frameworks and WHO resources.

Governance, leadership and investment requirements  Expanded content on governance, leadership, stewardship, stakeholder participation, funding and resourcing requirements for implementation and sustainability Barriers and enablers to  Added a dedicated section outlining implementation common barriers and enablers and potential strategies to address them Need for practical implementation supports  Developed the repository of tools and resources, implementation templates, worksheets and case studies to support application Equity and ethical considerations  Strengthened guidance relating to equity, priority populations, consumer engagement, data governance and ethical considerations Iterative and flexible implementation  Emphasised that LHS improvement processes are iterative, adaptive and non-linear, and that phases and steps may be blended, repeated, skipped or adapted to context

The development of the Guidance on using a LHS approach to implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-informed health interventions aimed to fill an important gap whereby limited practical guidance exists about how to translate LHS principles into action to support implementation, scale-up and sustainment efforts across varying health system levels, stakeholders, settings and resources (10, 12).

However, whilst evidence synthesis and expert advisory input are essential components of guidance development, they are insufficient on their own.

text.text: This identified the need to bridge potential gaps between technically sound recommendations and what can be implemented in real-world practice.

Stakeholders emphasised wording, language or assumptions that could affect interpretation, legitimacy and uptake of the Guidance given differences in values, priorities and needs across varying groups.
Strengths of the consultation include its structured and systematic approach, as well as the breadth of international stakeholders.
Participants included policymakers, researchers and practitioners from a range of relevant sectors and represented the six WHO regions.

The consultation was limited by an underrepresentation of some end-user groups (e.g., patients, consumers and community representatives) whose perspectives may have provided further realworld considerations.
The international stakeholder consultation provided a robust mechanism to assess the Guidance's relevance, usability, feasibility and acceptability.

To address this need, the World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with the University of Newcastle's National Centre of Implementation Science (NCOIS), developed a Guidance to using a Learning Health System's approach to implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-informed health interventions (henceforth referred to as the 'Guidance').

The Guidance aims to support organisations and interest-holders to use an LHS approach to strengthen the implementation, scale-up and sustainment of evidence-based interventions through continuous learning, adaptation and improvement.

Recommendations for Improving Guidance Content and Usability Stakeholders provided several recommendations to strengthen the content, presentation, and usability of the Guidance.

Stakeholders highlighted the importance of clearly defining LHSs and explaining how the proposed framework can be operationalised in practice, particularly that it is an iterative and adaptive process.
Stakeholders recommended including more practical examples, case studies, implementation tools, and resources to support application across different settings.
Participants also suggested that the Guidance should be written using clear and accessible language suitable for a broad audience, including policymakers, practitioners, managers, and researchers.
Feedback highlighted the importance of positioning the Guidance as strongly complementary to existing WHO frameworks and guidance documents to encourage its use and uptake.
Illustrative feedback "People are still struggling to understand what a learning health system is and how it links to policy processes."
"The linkage to some of the existing WHO and other global frameworks would be helpful."
"Consider how to better present it for non-academic audiences."
